utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will now begin the Prosecution's rebuttal. Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Would you call your first witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We call Sakib Sivac. SAKIB SIVAC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you testified previously in this matter. During your earlier testimony, you related to the Court that you were born and raised in Sivci, in opstina Prijedor ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- and discussed the cleansing of the male Muslim population from Sivci on June 14th 1992. I want to hand you a piece of paper and ask you if you know the person whose name appears on this piece of paper. If I may have the assistance of the usher? If you can show that to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. That is [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for not making my intentions clear, Mr. Sivac. I think we will ask for a redaction at this point. I am going to ask you, Mr. Sivac, to refer to this person as "Witness W" and I will be asking you questions about him using that initial. How did you happen to know Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first knew him from sight in Kozarac in passing, you know. Then later I was married up near his village. Between his village and from where my wife is, there is a mountain lodge and I used to go there with my father-in-law. We went there a few times. That is where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he a member of that mountaineering lodge or was he working there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if -- I was not a member, but I would go up there often. Anybody could go there on his own will. He was cleaning something and he brought some drinks to the table where myself and my father-in-law were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You related when you testified before the Court on an earlier occasion that after the cleansing of the male Muslim population from Sivci you were taken to Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see Witness W while you were in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was after about 25 to 30 days after my arrival in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that during daylight or at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was then -- at that time when I saw him was during the day time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you at that time, in what part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in No. 2, the whole time. Next to the right door when you enter from the scales, I was there by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you see Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the Witness W as he entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Witness W in civilian clothes or in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness was -- Witness W was in a uniform, the old SMB, and he was dirty as a pig from mud.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a rifle with a long butt, and it was a semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he come to Keraterm into room 2 to say "hello" to his former neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why he came, but when he entered, he and another one with him -- I did not know the other one, he had a short beard -- first he said, "Is there anybody from Brdjani here?" Nobody responded, so then he started swearing, cursing their balija mother. He said, "Fuck you, your Alija. We can't live together any more", and he trampled around the door a few metres perimeter on our feet and then he said, "Is there anybody here from Forici?" and nobody responded and then he walked out. There were four of the Foric's who were there who did not dare respond. Then he left and I do not know where he went later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it Witness W who asked for people from Brdjani and then began cursing Muslims when no one responded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that no one from Brdjani responded, and that when he asked for Foric's, although there were some there, they did not respond. Why did the Foric's not respond to the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not dare. They were afraid. They knew that they were not being called for anything good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you were transferred from Keraterm, were you taken to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you learn in Trnopolje camp whether there had also been members of the Foric family there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to Trnopolje, then they were saying that a lot of Foric's have been killed, that there were two by two, there were six of them, brothers, and then I saw my sister-in-law's brother and he said that ten of theirs were killed, father, brother, four sons, a wife, a daughter-in-law and two children, that many of the Foric's were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is all I have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Sivac being personally excused, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: This is really, I suppose, a question to you to save time. Can you show us where Brdjani and Forici is, just roughly, or tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: North, up toward the mountains from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are there additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Jusuf Arifagic. JUSUF ARIFAGIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your full name is Jusuf Arifagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You gave evidence before this Tribunal in this case on 8th August 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know a person who gave evidence in this case who had the pseudonym of Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want you to mention his name at any stage in the course of your testimony. Would you please have a look at this photograph that I now show you? Could you show it firstly to the Defence and then show it to the witness? Without mentioning the name, just looking at that, is that the person that you know as Witness W? Would you answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour, and might it be sealed, 363.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Any objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 363 will be admitted and sealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, how long have you known Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him almost my whole life. All the time that I lived in Kozarac, we were there together. I think he was a bit older than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period of the time that you lived in the Kozarac area, how often would you see him, regularly, rarely, or can you give us some idea of how often you came in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw him almost every day since he worked in Kozarac, so that my every visit to the town I had an opportunity to see him. I cannot say that it was every day, but on a weekly basis, two or three times at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what Witness W was doing during 1991, especially the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was in a part of the JNA -- I do not know if it was TO or not -- and I think that he took part in fighting around Pakrac and Lipik and that is what all his colleagues were saying, and he wore SMB uniform and carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you see him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Often times I would see him in passing, and on one occasion I was in a cafe with him and he was there in a uniform with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident in relation to a person called Mehmed Adzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that [redacted], apparently, threatened to throw a grenade, that he would throw a grenade in front of his house. I know that the man called his house, his brothers, and the man was coming and they had to pay attention, and the reason was because this man, Muhamed, was in the legal Territorial Defence of the former -- of the then JNA and that could have been one of the reasons why he wanted to throw a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you come to know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mehmed, Muhamed Mehmedagic's brother, was staying with me and we were talking about the situation in Kozarac and so he was telling me what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know this person Mehmedagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well. We were almost neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier an incident that you recall in a bar in Kozarac, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Whose bar was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the bar of Adil Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Witness W in this bar at the same time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who were you with at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting with friends in the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the mentioned person was with Adil Jakupovic and I think the other person's name was Muharem and they were quite -- he was quite drunk and at one point he said that he would activate a grenade in the bar and, obviously, there was a reaction on the part of others and Adil, as the owner, tried to calm the situation down, asked him to leave and they would go to the mountaineering lodge and that they would continue to drink there. But it all ended up by his leaving the bar and the police had to come and, apparently, he was taken to Prijedor, but the next day he reappeared with the uniform and the weapons in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he" on these occasions, you are referring to Witness W?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you mentioned "uniform", what uniform are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the SMB uniform of the old Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he returned the next day armed", again it was he, Witness W, who returned the next day armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened the next day when he returned to the bar armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One maybe needs to make a wider explanation. When I was sitting with this friend, I was building a family home, and he was doing part of the installation of electricity and that was one of the reasons why we were sitting in the bar and we were arranging about the work that needs to be done. The next morning, that same man came to my home and we started work and he told me, and I will try to quote, "There's that fool again drunk again. He came back from Prijedor, he has -- he is armed and he is going to avenge himself on all the people in Kozarac who framed him", so that he was taken to Prijedor, to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who Witness W associated with during the early part of 1992, some of the people that he associated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He associated mostly I think at that time still it was, it was still with all citizens in Kozarac, even though he in different incidents he caused reactions from other citizens. So he would often -- he could often be found in Dule's cafe and with other people who took part in fighting around Pakrac and Lipik, and there was knowledge. People in Kozarac knew about him. So this was not a short period of time, it was almost over a period of a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether the Muslim population in the Kozarac area taunted him or was rude to him or anything that you ever observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think no. If there were reactions, it was probably in response to his behaviour. In other words, people could not allow that he would behave the way he did. That day he wanted to activate a grenade in the cafe and this friend of mine was sitting with a little daughter who was, I think, I believe, about four years old. So it was all reactions to his bad behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Witness W in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was, approximately, that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in June sometime, or beginning of July -- in that period. In any event, I remember that he came to the camp and he was looking for people from Kozarac, from Brdjani, and apparently he wanted to see how we were and he even promised that the next morning he would bring us bread, but obviously he did not appear, nor bread. He was looking for certain people and made contacts with them. One of them was Namik Mahic. He asked him, "Where are -- where is Becir now?" I think he was thinking of Becir Medunjanin who was the President of SDA Party for Kozarac. Namik approached him and he said, "You know very well that I was in the TO, the legal TO, of Bosnia and Herzegovina and when everything started I took off the uniform and turned it in and I was not taking part in anything", and he said, "Don't be afraid, I will not harm you", or something in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Arifagic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you are permanently excused. That means you are free to leave. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a redaction at 10.22.08 ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Nasiha Klipic. NASIHA KLIPIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your full name Nasiha Klipic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you previously give evidence before the Tribunal in respect of this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the photograph that I now show you, please? Could it be shown to the Defence first, please? Madam, would you look at this photograph, please, and can you tell me, do you recognise the person that you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Zeljko Maric, a traffic policeman from Donji Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long have you known him, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known him since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him because he was always on the same duty between Kozarac and Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What duty was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was working as a traffic policeman at a point, Kozarac/Kamicani -- it depended -- but before the war he was mostly in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, your Honour, given the number 364.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 364 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, did you know Zeljko Maric in a social way, socially? Did you and your husband socialise with him at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this occasionally or often or rarely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the war, were you and your husband friendly with Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we used to go very often to cafe bars, listen to music and he was going out with a friend of mine. We used to go swimming in the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know some of the friends of Zeljko Maric prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Maric was on good terms with all the policemen. Emir Karabasic was once with us when we went swimming in the Sana River. There was my husband, myself, Zeljko Maric and a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Emir Karabasic a friend of Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what work, in particular, what duties Zeljko Maric was performing in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early part of 1992, Zeljko Maric, Zeljko Ignatovic, Cigo, the traffic policeman, and there were two soldiers and then two Muslim policemen just before the war had a joint checkpoint. They worked together there in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this a fixed checkpoint or did they move from place to place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the war it was a fixed, permanent checkpoint and before the war it was in Kozarusa, Susici. It depended. Traffic policemen would just stop somewhere and then they would stop a car sometimes in Kamicani sometimes -- it depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, in the early part of 1992 it was not a fixed checkpoint, but then just prior to the war in 1992 it became a fixed checkpoint that he worked at, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Previously when you gave evidence you spoke of being a part of a large column of people that went down through the main street of Kozarac, and then went towards Velika Kozarusa. Do you remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that that incident when you were in that column was on 27th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that day, did you see Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also in Kozarusa, there in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What group is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarusa where people were being separated by Ziko's cafe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was he doing, could you see, Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him. He was working -- he was doing just the same things as the others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he in uniform on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What uniform did he have on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They still had their loyal uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the "loyal uniform", can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same one as my husband used to wear before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your husband was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So he had a police uniform on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he armed on that occasion, Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every policemen at that time had a pistol and an automatic rifle. The policemen used to have it before the war and just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw Zeljko Maric at this place, did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him at any stage on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day, but in the SUP in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. When did you have a conversation with him in the SUP in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back from the Trnopolje camp, it was on 8th or 10th June, and then I continued to live in Prijedor until 28th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it was it sometime in June that you had a conversation with him in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you relate the conversation that you had with him for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just met before the SUP building and he said, "Where are you, Klipic? What is new?" "Nothing", said I. "Do you know anything about our policemen, where they?" "Nothing". I said, "Please be human; you are a policeman. You have also got two children", I think there were two sons, "just as I have got two children and I heard that my husband was killed with these eleven other policemen I heard, and please allow me at least to bury him". He told me, "Nasiha, I would really like to take you there, but he was certainly not killed there. There were people who were killed but he was not killed there".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were told he was not killed there. Where was "there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the printers in Kozarac, where the junction is. Some eleven policemen were shot there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Klipic, you indicated that when you saw Mr. Maric at Kozarusa that he was doing what the others were doing. What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Separating people. Normally there was a group there. You understand? I did not know where they were separating, what to do, and then basically they were separating everybody. Some people went to Keraterm or Trnopolje or Omarska. I do not know who allocated who to go where. I could not see it but I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Klipic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Klipic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am looking at my notes. I meant to ask Mrs. Klipic when she said that there were people who were killed there, did she know who had killed them? I do not remember whether that came from her previous testimony. Of course, she has now left and been permanently excused and I can check her previous testimony, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will have it checked, your Honour, but she can be recalled, I think, on that without any difficulty. I will just ask somebody to go through the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Advija Campara, your Honour. ADVIJA CAMPARA, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Advija Campara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and I have one child.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hajrudin Campara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that in the opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the opstina of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, where did you live -- I am sorry. When were you married? When were you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac. I used to live in Jakupovici up until 1979. Then after that I moved in Kozarac in the Skender Kulenovic street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that otherwise sometimes referred to as Kalate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you live at Kalate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live there with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your husband's occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did he teach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the primary school, Rade Kondic, in Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that primary school in any way connected with the elementary school in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the connection between the two schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, it is all really Kozarac, in Kozarac, but in Kamicani it was just the first four classes, and after that in Kozarac they were all eight classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So there was a direct link between the two schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How is it that you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in Kozarac it is impossible not to know somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some stage did you live near the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he lived in the same street where I used to live, Skender Kulenovic Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is when you lived in Kalate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many houses away from your house was the house of Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fourth house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was he living there with at the time when you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his wife Mira and two children. In fact, I do not know exactly whether at that time he had two children or just one. I know that the elder daughter was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This house that Dule Tadic lived in, do you know who owned that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the house of Ahmet Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know Dule Tadic's wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. She used to work at the Kozarac hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was her name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mira.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did Mira do at the Kozarac hospital? What was her job, did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you mentioned earlier that Dule and Mira Tadic had two children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was one of the children close to the age of your daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, maybe a year older than my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you then live after 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, in Pecani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you give the full address of the property in Pecani, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was Pecani C1, entrance 3. The number of the apartment was 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the telephone number of that apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How is it that you came to get this apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 30 years of working in the Rade Kondic school, my husband acquired the right to get that flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this the system that operated in Yugoslavia when Tito was the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did people become entitled to certain things after numbers of years of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were points that were given and those people who had the greatest number of points would be allocated an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When these apartments were allocated, what was the process? How did you go about obtaining it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The council had to meet, and then they would see who had the greatest number of points, that person was allocated an apartment. We all had to go through that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were allocated an apartment, how long were you allowed to stay there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of your life. Even our child would have the right to inherit it in case he would have lived with us till our death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you pay any rent or maintenance for these apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that at first it was some three and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was this money paid for? What was the purpose of paying the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was for maintenance of the building, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you allowed to carry out improvements to these apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, it was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you carry out improvements to this apartment that you were allocated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in 1990 we put a new parquet floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a nice apartment from the point of view of ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- the sort of standard of apartments in Prijedor? Was it a nice apartment based on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a new apartment, rather nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at this photograph for me, please. Might the photograph firstly be shown to the Defence? Madam, would you look at that photograph and can you tell me if you recognise the person in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the man who threw me out of the apartment, Rajko Karanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you first see this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 10th July 1992 when he knocked at my door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, if your Honour pleases?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 365 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, what was the first day and date that you saw this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 10th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What day was that, day of the week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At approximately what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around half past one in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us, were you alone at that time or were you with somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not alone. There was another woman there and five children under the age of 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your daughter there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How old was your daughter at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was not quite 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was your husband at this time, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened at 1.30 on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three men came, three armed men. They were knocking with their boots on the door. That was the way they were used to do it, kicking the door with their boots. That was the way people used to enter. There was no electricity so that they could ring the bell. The first person who entered -- I did not know at the time who he was -- was Rajko Karanovic. After him there was a second man who came in, and the third one did not want to come in when he saw that there were women and children there. He remained in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the two men then entered the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they carrying any arms or weapons with them at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice at that time the weapons when they came in, but the first thing I noticed was a knife because Rajko, when he entered in the corridor, he took the knife out and he started hitting the shelf on which the telephone was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "hitting", what do you mean "hitting"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he entered in that corridor he took the knife out and he started sort of hitting on the shelf. There was a small note there on the telephone directory. He put that -- he put that piece of paper on the knife. Then he asked me whose telephone number was that, of what Ustasha with which I was collaborating it was the number of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he hitting with the knife or stabbing with the knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stabbing with the knife. I think that on the shelf there are visible traces of that. One could see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were these men dressed, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rajko was wearing the olive green uniform. The other one was wearing a camouflage uniform. He also had some kind of an insignia on his sleeve. I think it was the sign of -- the insignia of the white eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say he had the insignia of the white eagle, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second person that came with Rajko, by the name of Stevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So Stevo had the white eagle insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise the uniform that Rajko was wearing, what that uniform was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the old uniform of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from stabbing the note with the knife and asking you questions, did he do anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then he went behind the dining room table. Then he took a piece of paper out and told me that was a decision for the allocation of flat and I thought that he wanted me to read it so that I could -- he wanted to show it to me, and he turned it away so that I could see what was on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go and look at this piece of paper he had? Did he offer it to you to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but when I came towards him he turned this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say he "turned" it, did he prevent you from looking at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from stabbing the note on the shelf, did he stab anything else in the room with his knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the shelf, on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may raise one matter? I know my ability with the language is not that recognised but, as I understood the answer in relation to preventing from looking at the note, the witness replied "ne" and said it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will raise it again with the witness. [To the witness]: When you say that Rajko turned the paper away, are you saying that he tried to prevent you from looking at the paper or was he showing it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was speaking clearly. He did not allow me to see the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you try to look at the piece of paper that he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I came there by him and when I came near him, then he turned it around and saying it was a decision. He did not want me to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see what was written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from stabbing the note on the telephone shelf, did he stab anything else with his knife when he was in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this piece of paper that was there on the telephone directory. He put it on the knife and turned it around and he asked me whose number that was. I did not know whose number that was. He was asking, who were these Ustashas we were collaborating with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he do anything with the furniture in the apartment when he came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came near. He opened all the drawers in the chest of drawers and he was trying to see whether there was some kind of an explosive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that he was trying to see if there was some sort of an explosive there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were maybe half a metre, one from the other. He opened three drawers. There were three drawers. He was opening them one by one. He was trying to see what was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you when he was opening these drawers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was trying to see whether I did not put any explosives in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you when he was opening these drawers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He only said that, that he was trying to see whether I did not put any explosives in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So he mentioned the word "explosives", did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he then say anything to you about leaving the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they told me that I could stay there until the next morning in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. I kept silent. I had nothing to say. Maybe after a minute maybe, Stevo took me to the bedroom and Rajko gave him a sign with his eyes and he put the automatic rifle barrel on to my temple. There was a baby sleeping there. He said if I did not leave that I would go there with -- that I would be taken to Omarska with this baby because that is where the Muslims belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took you to the bedroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who gave the sign with his eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Rajko give the sign to Stevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, apparently, it was too long a period of time for him that I should be there until the next morning so they wanted to speed it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went into the bedroom were you alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was a three month old baby sleeping in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the baby, was there anyone else in the bedroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just myself and Stevo, and when I started crying then my daughter came to the door. She came in running. She started crying very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When your daughter came into the room, did Stevo still have the gun to your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My daughter started crying and she said, "Mum, do we have to leave the apartment?" and I said, "Yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in the bedroom or did you leave the bedroom at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we left at that point. We left ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- and then my daughter said, "Mum, they took our father first. Where are we going to go, you and I?" Then Rajko came and he took her like this, raised her chin and he said, "Little one, you will make a grave mistake if you miss your profession. You should be an actress".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they then say to you what time you had to leave the apartment by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Rajko pointed like this and he said, "When I get here at 5.30, I want to see the apartment empty, but I will come once before that to make sure that you are getting ready to leave".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he came back later that day? Did Rajko come back later that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he armed again the next time he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember what weapons he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had automatic weapons, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he with anyone the next time he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, again Stevo came with him and that third one, and again the third one stayed in the hallway in front of the door. He did not enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just before they had come back, did you receive some help from your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my neighbour came who was a Serb, and he called the Crisis Staff and he said, "Just spare at least women and children. Don't expel women and children", and then he told me what they told him, not to get involved too much because he could end up like I did. He told me that I had to leave, that I could not stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you just mentioned that Rajko came back before 5.30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came around, between 3.30 and 4.00 again, and he wanted to see the decision of the allocation for the apartment that I had that were in our possession, I told him that I had no documents, that I did not know where they were and then he sort of ironically said, "Well, you never had it anyway".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, have the documents for the apartment at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I did. I had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you leave the apartment then at 5.30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came maybe five minutes before 5.30, again Stevo and Rajko, but I want to add, every time they would come they would be more and more drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go back to the apartment the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I came in the morning around 9.00 o'clock, since in that hurry we did not manage to take the basic things. My daughter had a long hair and we did not have a brush, and in the morning we could not brush her hair. So we went looking for the hair brush. We knocked on the door and a man opened up with a beard and he was -- he had a stench from alcohol and later I found out that he was Rajko's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with this man or did you just leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was a hair brush in the hallway and I just picked it up and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then go to the SUP to see what you could do about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was Saturday, and only on Monday I went to the SUP, on 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you went to the SUP on 13th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came and they told me to wait, to go -- but there was already a party in the room. I think it was room No. 2 or 3. I do not recall. I waited there for a while. When I entered the room 2 or 3, my neighbour was sitting there. His name is Tomo and he was a policeman. He used to work in the SUP previously. At first he pretended he did not recognise me, and he said, "Why, have I changed so much? I have lost weight", and I told him what happened. But I want to say just one thing: on the same day, Rajko changed the lock on the door. He came with a person and changed the lock. I had the keys, but I actually would not dare come back. Then Tomo told me that I should go and break into the apartment, and I said, "Give me a man" and he said, "No, we will not risk our people. The people who threw you out are ready for anything", and he said, "So what? Are you asking me to go there and get killed?" He said nothing. In fact, he said to go to Pecani, and there was a place where we could go to and complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then go and see at a later stage the military police about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, later, only later, did I go to the military police. I first went to Pecani on 14th and that person there, Dragan, who was working in that police there, he said, "It is good. You fared well because sometimes we beat up people who behave like that".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Behaved like what, did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me, "It is good that you were not beaten up because we can beat up people who do not obey the orders". On that -- then I left Pecani and I moved to Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go at some stage then to see the military police about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the military police. I do not know exactly the date, I do not recall, but I think it was towards the end of July, and they told me that there was a person by the name of Radetic, Dragan, that he was in charge, that he will help. I think he was also with the military police. I knew where his parent's house was. I went there and his mother sent me to the military police. I had never been to Cirkin Polje. I did not know where that was. There was a road passed Keraterm. You turn right and there was a large group. That is when I went to the military police. There was a large group of soldiers, 50 or 60 of them. They were going somewhere, and that is where I met Ika, Ika, Ante Murgic's wife. Ante was killed and also her son and I had not seen that, and she started crying and then she mentioned -- she said, "Dusko Tadic killed my Zoran and my Ante". I was -- I got very scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Rather than go into that, can you just tell us what had happened when you made your enquiries at the military police? Did they help you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were very civil. They received me very well and they heard me out. I returned then. I was at that time in Raskovac. Towards the evening, my neighbour called me and said that the military police had come and that they left a note saying that Rajko could not stay in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone from the military police about your apartment or did you just receive a note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received a message and, in fact, he never moved in. They wrote on the door that he could not and there was a notice and I saw it. I went to my neighbours who lived on the same floor where I lived and it said there that nobody could move into that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was signed by the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Cyrillic. I remember well. It was in the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why Rajko was not permitted to move into the premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at that time whoever was only on duty within the city of Prijedor could not, but he brought Stevo with him and Stevo had been on all fronts, and he said it was not for nothing that he got a declaration that he had on the left sleeve, and that was a problem and Rajko had no basis, he was lying, he had nothing, he had no decisions, no documents that he could move into the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, I just want you to tell me what you mean by saying that whoever was on duty within the city could not obtain the apartment. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what I mean is that was to raise their morals. Whoever would enlist to go to the front, they could get anything, or somebody who would be either in the SUP or in the Crisis Staff, they could get it. But since Rajko was just a common soldier who was just on duty on these checkpoints, he could not get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So are you saying that the allocation of apartments was based on whether or not people had fought at the front or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even though -- or if he held a high position within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you later see Stevo? On another occasion later on did you meet with Stevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was that approximately, how much later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had Rajko moved into the apartment by this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you meet Stevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the house of Sado and Timka who lived in Raskovici. I do not know their last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Stevo recognise you when he first saw you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevo came with Aco. I do not know his last name, but I know that he was a driver for the municipality. So Aco first came in and Stevo behind him and he did not know -- he only knew Timka but not Sado, because Aco was their house friends. He first extended his arm. He said, "Do I know you from somewhere?" I said, "We know each other quite well".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say "he first extended his arm", you mean he put his arm out to shake your hand, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was when he did that that he said, "Do we know each other?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he looked at me, because I was not looking at him up until then, I only looked at him when he extended his hand and then he said, "Do we know each other from somewhere?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you tell him from where it was that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then I told him, "You see, Stevo, how we meet, sometimes you don't think", and maybe that could have cost me. I said, "See how we met and maybe you will meet me at some point where you would not like to meet me". He said nothing. He just nodded and he looked at me. Then I told him, "Why did Rajko not move into the apartment?" He said, "Well, there are other things that need to be resolved", and he said, "but Dusko will help him. Dusko is now the first man in Kozarac".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "Dusko"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How is it that Dusko Tadic could help you, did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think because it was the apartment belonged to the Rade Kondic school and the documents I later found out, the documents were moved to the kindergarten. Then they were looking -- he was looking for ways, and I think that Stevo knew, since he told me, and he knew that I knew Dusko, Stevo must have recommended Dusko to help him and at that time this Local Commune was established in Kozarac. I do not know how they called it, but Dusko was the first person on it. It was like a municipality or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Rajko eventually moved into the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think some time in the beginning of September or end of August. In any event, he did not move in for about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then later return to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only in December when I was about to leave Prijedor, I think on 13th or 14th -- the 13th December, I went with a friend from Banja Luka who was a Serb. He came to take some things from me because I had taken nothing out of the apartment, and all the time up until then I believed, I had hoped, that I would return to the apartment, I would stay there, and we went there sometime in the afternoon to Rajko's door. I rang the bell. Vera came out. She did not know me. I introduced myself. I said I was Advija. She just turned her head and called Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was Vera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rajko's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Did Rajko then come to the door when she called him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he came to the door what did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that this man who was with me, that he wanted to take some things, that I came for my belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did Rajko say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he distributed all the things to the Serb refugees. Then I looked him in the face and then I dropped my look and he was standing on my rug, and he said that there was not a piece of cloth left, that he had given everything away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that the last time you ever went to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During 1992, the year of 1992, were you ever in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you there alone or was your daughter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My daughter as well as my brother's two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was it that you were in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there on 27th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 25th or 26th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Trnopolje camp, were there any guards or people armed surrounding the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what nationality these people were that were guarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were they dressed, the people that were surrounding the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say that they were motley. They were all kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did policemen or soldiers who were not guards at the camp enter the camp from time to time, did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the daily routine. They could do whatever they want. They entered whenever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people that entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you name some of the people that you saw enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very many, there are many names. There was Zuna from Radivojci which is really Petrov Gaj; Novo, Dule Tadic -- many, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often did you see Dule Tadic enter the camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly, but very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he entered the camp how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he had an overall like a military uniform and sometimes a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you notice whether he was carrying any arms when he entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, always.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise what arms he was carrying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the weapons very well. It was not a very long barrel. It was an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw Dule Tadic at the camp, did he actually come into the camp or was he staying on the outside on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time when I saw him when he came he was in the school building itself. He was looking for somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone telling you anything about a building near the camp, a house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was when I came to visit Trnopolje before I went to the camp. On one occasion there was a group of women and we were going there and a bus came from Omarska. I was expecting my husband's release at the time and when we arrived just at the camp, maybe about 200, 300 metres from the school building, it was very hot, and a woman invited us to come and rest there, because we were going on bicycles. At that time Serbs had started moving into Trnopolje. I thought that she was a Serb. I did not know that there were any old inhabitants in the houses, and so I asked why she was there and she said, "I should have left", and I should say that the house had not been finished. The top floor was without windows and he said that the night before they brought in a girl with them and that they had their way with her all night, and they said that -- then she said that she should have left and that she was going to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The house that you are talking about, that was not the house where this woman who offered you hospitality but it was a house nearby, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the woman -- she gave us water, she had nothing else, and she called to us to come and rest and take a glass of water and at that time she told us this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the house she was talking about was not her house, it was the house nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was her house. We were standing in front of her house. I do not know if it used to belong to her originally or if she was a refugee, but she was saying that this had happened in this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. You saw this ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could object to something, your Honour? This is supposed to be a part of the Prosecution case which is in rebuttal of the Defence which we have recently heard over some six or seven weeks. At the moment, I fail to understand how this is in rebuttal of any aspect of the Defence case. As I recollect developments during the Defence, the Prosecution, in fact, withdrew allegations concerning Trnopolje that had been made against the defendant Dusko Tadic on the basis that those allegations had been falsified by one of their witnesses. I am at a loss at this stage to understand how any aspect of this evidence is in rebuttal of any part of the Defence case at all, or whether we are hearing yet again more stories recounted through other witnesses that are not relevant to this defendant.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness should be asked, your Honour, to remove the headset?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mrs. Campara, would you remove your earphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is that very matter, your Honour, that prompts us to raise these issues relevant to Trnopolje, because the allegations specifically in relation to the witness that Mr. Kay has referred to certainly have been withdrawn by the Prosecution in relation to paragraph 4.3 of the indictment. But, your Honour, it is our allegation that the count of persecution which incorporates, not only Omarska and the Keraterm camp, but also includes the camp at Trnopolje, and they are still live and the period of time leading up until December is still live. The Prosecution have not in any way attempted to withdraw that count of persecution at that time frame in relation to that place. It is because, in our submission, that there is this suggestion that the whole of the allegation relevant to Trnopolje has been withdrawn that this material is relevant now in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay had said that the Prosecution was dropping allegations regarding Trnopolje. That is not your position, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Our position has always been those allegations contain specifically in 4.3 where I highlighted ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are beyond recess time so we will stand in recess for 20 minutes and then we will return with the ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. During the break and having a chance to consider what Mr. Niemann raised to your Honour concerning 4.3 in the indictment, can we remind the Court that the indictment was only extended as a result of the application by the Prosecution based on the statement and the evidence they wish to adduce through Witness L, (redacted)? That was a specific application made by the Prosecution to enable them to extend the period of time in which the indictment against the defendant Tadic was moved from, I believe, the end of August 1992 until 31st December 1992. Looking at paragraph 4.3, your Honour will notice that the wording as remaining is that "During the period between 25th May 1992 and 31st December 1992 Dusko Tadic physically participated and otherwise assisted in the transfer to an unlawful confinement in Trnopolje camp of non-Serb persons from the Kozarac area". It seems the testimony we are hearing from this particular witness, if it had any impact at all, should have been evidence that was called as part of the first stage of the Prosecution case when they were making their allegations and presenting evidence in support of the indictment. What we have been hearing from this witness, however, in our submission, does not fit into that context at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You seem to be raising two points, and I do not recall the -- you are talking about the application to amend the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I do not recall whether the request to amend the indictment to extend it from August to December '92 was limited to or based on only the testimony of Witness L. So, since the Prosecution has withdrawn Witness L, then it would be your position that, even if Trnopolje is still an issue, it would extend only until August '92 and not go to December '92. That is one issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the second issue is just a pure question of whether this is truly rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even if it were limited to August '92, is it really appropriately rebuttal evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had several other witnesses, though, who testified about Trnopolje. Dr. Gutic was one; he was there, as I recall -- I did not look at it -- at least through the fall of '92. I do not why I am thinking October, but at least through the fall. I do not know whether he was there in December. I just do not remember. We have had other testimony regarding Trnopolje at other periods. I suppose we could go back and see whether the only testimony to go beyond August '92 would have been Witness L. I just do not have that kind of grasp, except I am almost positive that Dr. Gutic was talking about the fall of '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He is the one I remember because he gave so much testimony on Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can perhaps assist your Honour with my recollection concerning the other witnesses. There was Mr. Adil Jakupovic who was there until the ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- 2nd December '92 who said that he saw Dusko Tadic there, I believe, on one occasion. There was his wife, Nasiha Jakupovic, who may have given testimony to a similar degree. At that stage it was all pre-Witness L evidence. What we are considering in 4.3 is the wording "physically participated and otherwise assisted in the transfer to an unlawful confinement in Trnopolje camp of non-Serb persons". Our submission is that what we are hearing now at this stage is not rebuttal, and I also link it to this specific point because the Court may be concerned with relevancy at this stage to these matters that we say do not assist the Court in relation to the allegations within the indictment. If we had wanted to continue with our evidence concerning Trnopolje, we could have done so. We actually limited the evidence from our investigator, Mr. Petrovic, who could have advised the Court further about the surrounding area of Trnopolje, all focused upon the Witness L, (redacted), testimony and the products of his research in relation to those allegations. Because it was seen as being a dead issue by that stage, we, of course, limited the material that we produced before the Court because there was no point. There is no point in us dealing with those allegations from him because we were no longer concerned with them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, I do not recall Witness L testifying that Mr. Tadic participated or otherwise assisted in the transfer ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- of persons to Trnopolje camp anyway. That is alleged in 4.3. Maybe he did. But I never understood that the Trnopolje issue was out of the case because of the Prosecution's decision no longer to rely on the testimony of Witness L as being truthful, because there are many witnesses who have testified about Trnopolje and in paragraph 4 you have allegations regarding Trnopolje ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- which do not relate to L.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Anyway, we have heard a lot of witnesses, but let us see what the Prosecution has to say. Let me ask you, is it your position that Trnopolje is not an issue in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it is within count 1, the persecution count. We do not seek to avoid that, but the evidence we are hearing now should have been called at the first stage of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the second issue. OK. Mr. Niemann, what evidence offered by the Defence would this proposed testimony of the witness be designed to rebut?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence of the Defence suggests a number of things in relation to Mr. Tadic's attendance at or participation in Trnopolje camp. Included among those things is attending the camp in relation to the humanitarian reasons connected with the Red Cross, connected with discussions with the witnesses about housing.
