There is also a suggestion arising from the Defence evidence that the Kozarac police had no jurisdiction in the area, so he could not have come there on official business because the police simply had no jurisdiction over the Trnopolje camp; that, in fact, was allocated to another police force. In addition to that, your Honours, there is evidence that the Defence put on in their case that he was so busily employed and involved with the commission of housing, the housing commission enquiry that was going on during this relevant period, that really he would not have had much time to do anything else but to attend to these duties. So these are the impressions that were created by the Defence case which this evidence is intended to address. Dealing, your Honour, with the question of this idea that the date leading up to December 31st is limited only to Witness L's testimony. That is simply not correct. It was not only Witness L's testimony that brought about the amendment. We submitted 22 statements in relation to this amendment to the indictment on 1st September 1995. The witness Adil Jakupovic speaks of the accused being at the camp in December '92 and Jusuf Arifagic also gave evidence that he was there on 1st October 1992. So there is some evidence in relation to that. But this evidence is called, particularly the evidence of visits to the camp is called, to rebut that impression created by the Defence that he was only there on a couple of occasions; when he went there, he certainly could not have gone there on police duty and he was there for humanitarian reasons and, indeed, he was so busily occupied with his housing commission duties that he simply could not really have had much time to get there. That is the purpose of it, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding the limitation period, December 22nd, you have indicated that you submitted 22, did you say, witness statements? Of course, this Chamber would not know about that since the proposed amendment would go to the confirming Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But our concern really is what this evidence is designed to rebut. I think everything that you say is true, and that is that there was testimony from the Defence that Mr. Tadic's duties were as you have said in his visits and the question of whether he was really even on the camp grounds proper. But the proposed testimony of Mrs. Campara deals with hearsay, which of course is not a problem in the Chamber, but regarding rapes that occurred at a particular house, and I do not know how far she is going to get with that, but at that point, at least, that does not implicate Mr. Tadic ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, not at all, your Honour, not in relation to those events.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- on the camp grounds. So that sounds more like the kind of testimony that Dr. Gutic gave and it sounds more like the kind of evidence that you could have adduced during your case in chief. Our concern is that this not be a practise of offering additional evidence that you would have had an opportunity to offer on the case in chief. So the specific testimony that she is about to offer does not appear to rebut any of those things, because she is not going to say that she saw Mr. Tadic then participate in these. She has already said that she saw him in the school which would be the camp proper. I do not think it deals with the other issues. So, we will find that this does go beyond the Defence's case, that it is not rebuttal of any of the evidence but new evidence that could have been elicited during the Prosecution's case in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for my guidance, am I permitted to ask questions about Mr. Tadic being at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. That clearly has been raised by the Defence, and where he was, what he was doing etc., yes. OK. Would you ask Mrs. Campara to return? MRS. ADVIJA CAMPARA, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, before the morning adjournment, you had told us in the course of your evidence that during the period of time that you were in the Trnopolje camp, from late September through to the end of November, you had seen the accused Dule Tadic come into the camp on quite a number -- I think you said quite often, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us approximately how many times you think it is that you saw him enter the camp? I know it is not easy to remember precisely, but can you give us a figure which you think is close to the number of times you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can very -- with certainty state that that was more than 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say him enter the camp during this period, was he on his own or was he with other people or was it a mixture of ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he was on his own. It depended; sometimes on his own, sometimes in the company of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he came to the camp, did he always come into the camp itself or did he just come to the area or was it a mixture of both on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time I saw him in the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "in the camp", is there any particular part of the camp that you saw him go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was still warmer when I would go outside, I had with me two small children of my brother, otherwise we were at the school. I see him outside but very often also inside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you be provided with a piece of paper and write down on it the country in which you are presently living at the moment and the name of the town? Could you write down the name of the particular country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I live at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I did not write it sort of very clearly, but I did write that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be shown to the Prosecution and then to the Court? Then it would, perhaps, be appropriate to seal it as an Exhibit, your Honour, as the next Defence Exhibit which would be D103.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 103?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be admitted and sealed. MR. KAY (To the witness): Can you tell us, please, when you were first asked to be a witness in this case, if you could give me the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean? What date? When I had my first interview? I do not quite understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you been interviewed then by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What month was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When were you asked to be a witness in the case of the Prosecution against Dusko Tadic? You do not have to give me the precise day, just the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was somewhere in November, end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of this year, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in September, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before you were asked to be a witness, had you seen any of the proceedings on television in that country where you are living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, [redacted] does not present anything about Bosnia, so I have no opportunity to see any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you read anything about it in the newspapers in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think my head is full of everything for my whole life. I do not think I need anything else to remind me of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that country where you are living in has not had any of the proceedings against Dusko Tadic in this Court on television, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not even watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you have a television where you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a television, but I do not watch it at all. I do not speak the language well at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But some of the witnesses giving evidence in this Court have been speaking in your own language of Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mostly do not watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But originally you said there was nothing about this case on the television in the country ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can state there with certainty that [redacted] does not show any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not in any of the news programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Maybe at first when the trial had actually started, maybe they just only mentioned that the trial was starting. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the trial against Mr. Tadic started, had you seen any programmes on [redacted] making allegations against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have given us your married name. What is your own family name, your name before you were married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you related to Adil Jakupovic or Nasiha Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with Adil. He comes from the same village I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is he a blood relative of yours or are you distant cousins? What is the connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say. He is a relative, not really a close one, but a relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know his family well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know his wife Nasiha well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see her these days? Have you seen her recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not after, after I left Prijedor, I have not, and I do not know where she lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you spoken to her at all, perhaps on the telephone or any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can tell you I do not really know where she lives, where she is at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you a few questions about what happened to you in Prijedor in relation to the flat that you had in Pecani. You mentioned a man called Stevo. Do you know what his last name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did know his last name but I know he comes from Gomjenac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what his job was, what his employment was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described him as being present when your flat was taken from you. Did you know then ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- what his job was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I could have supposed that he was there in order to help Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he have any official capacity to help the man Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they have known each other from before. Later on I heard that Rajko picked him up at a cafe. First, they had drinks and then Rajko told him, "Come with me to help me, to help me, I need you to do some job". That was told to me by a neighbour of mine, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems that Rajko was using this man as some sort of physical support rather than any official capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both, because there was a reason why he showed the insignia on his sleeve saying that he was on all the front lines and there was for good reason that he earned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But that was the man Stevo who had been on the front lines, not the man Rajko Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Stevo had been on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What Stevo was doing there was boasting about his military involvement rather than any official position he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he would not have been able to get that insignia had he not held some official duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The insignia you refer to, is it a rank or a badge of office? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. As much as I could see at that moment. I remember because he was very near me. I was sitting on my daughter's bed and he was, I think, at that time on his knees because he was holding the automatic rifle. So we must have been at the same sort of height and his left hand was near me and, as much as I could see, it was red and white in colour. Maybe at that moment -- but there was something like the white eagles, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But, so far as you could tell, his only involvement came about because he was met in a bar and told to come along rather than because he was appointed to help the man Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said a neighbour had told you that Karanovic had met him in a bar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but Karanovic could not just come and pick up just anybody, that is, he knew who he was going to take along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The piece of paper, you say, was never seen by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see it. It was -- this woman that was living with me, my cousin's wife, she was staying with me, and the telephone number was the one of her parents' house. Her parents lived in Puharska. Some 10 minutes before they came to expel me, she was on the phone and so she jotted down that phone number in order to be able to phone them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Dusko Tadic was evicted from his flat in Pecani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what flat you mean. What Dusko Tadic's flat in Pecani?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw this man Stevo again, how long after the taking of your flat was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some, I think, end of July, early August, somewhere during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you see this man then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Raskovaci, in Timka's and Sado's house. I do not know their last name. But I know that that man was released from Omarska, that man Sado.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The place you have told us about, Raskovaci, whereabouts is that in relation to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- how can I explain -- just behind the old town, what used to be the old town before. Now it does not exist any more. There is a road that leads to the road Bosanski Novi/Prijedor, and there you have got the Raskovac part of the town. While I was in Pecani, there was only a canal separating us. In fact, it is a part of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It is a part of Prijedor that exists near the road that would take you out to Bosanski Novi, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw this man on this occasion, was he taking someone else's house then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Then he came to visit Timka and Sado. He was with Aco. I only know Aco by his first name. I do not know his last name. I know he was a driver at the town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he a friend of your friends at Raskovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aco, yes, and Stevo was there for the first time, because Stevo was later on the checkpoint just behind Raskovac, at the very end of the street in Raskovac, which takes you to the road Prijedor/Bosanski Novi, and probably whilst going back home from the checkpoint he came to see with Aco, he came to see Timka and Sado.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was he a soldier then on the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was a group of them and I think that he was the head of them. There was not just one soldier at the checkpoint. There were several soldiers and then there was also somebody who was in charge of the soldiers. I think he had some kind of a duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then did you learn that he worked at this checkpoint guarding the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that out beforehand. My daughter once went to the store with my neighbour, because there was a discount place -- it was about 1.5 kilometres from where I lived -- and when she returned she was all blushing and she said there was that man who threw us out of the apartment down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, it does not seem then that he was involved in politics within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean by "active". In fact, you need to clarify it a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He does not seem to have had any job or position within the municipality in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never said that he had a position in the Prijedor municipality; only that he came with the man who was driving for the municipality. He came alongside with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, it seems then you agree with what I have asked you about, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What point you are making?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please allow me to make the points. If you can just answer the questions and not think I am making any points. He does not have any job then, so far as you know, within the municipality of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never once mentioned the municipality of Kozarac, only the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could answer the question from what you learnt about him? He did not seem to have any position within the municipality of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can answer the question, if you can?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this Stevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what connection Stevo may have and the municipality of Kozarac. When we were talking about the municipality of Prijedor, we talked about how he came and who he came with, how I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you wanted some assistance, if the witness could take her headphones off, I can explain to the Court. I think your Honour probably understands why I am asking the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. (To the witness): I would like to ask you some questions now about Trnopolje. That was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness has taken her headphones off.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Campara, you may put your headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now about Trnopolje which was a place that you stayed in from, I believe you told us, the end of September until 25th or 26th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before that you had visited Trnopolje on how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was your first visit to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall the date exactly, whether in the period when I was there, I think that we went on foot. I think that a group of women from Puharksa from the 14th and 21st of July, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your visit to Trnopolje in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group from Omarska arrived -- in fact, at that time they did not come. There were stories. We were always expecting somebody to call, but that was all false information. So, apparently, a group arrived. So, obviously, I went to see if my husband arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have to have any special permission to travel to Trnopolje on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right away on 14th. In fact on 13th when I went to the SUP I had to take out a permit with my name and my sister-in-law's and the children so we could move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The purpose of that permit was to show at checkpoints the reason for your journey and where you were going, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your second visit to Trnopolje, can you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe end of June. I had already move moved to Raskovac. I know once I went from Puharska in that period of between the 14th and 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your visit to Trnopolje on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same purpose. Again, in fact at that time one group did arrive from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The third visit to Trnopolje, what was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again the same kind of visit. Again I went to see whether my husband arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly when the Keraterm camp was dissolved. I know that at that time there was a group that came from Omarska. Keraterm had been dissolved and one group of people was moved from Keraterm to Trnopolje. For one group it was never found out where they went. There was a cousin, I did not know about him until the war broke out, so when I went to Trnopolje once I found this cousin who had come from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As on first visit, for the other visits did you have the same certificates to permit you to travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was free movement. That is what the permit was called. If you got it from the SUP you could move around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you could only go to that place where the certificate said you were going, which would have been a permit that permitted you to travel to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not only Trnopolje. It was just freedom of movement. That is what it said on the permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it say on the permit where you were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to these visits, how long did you stay at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An hour or two, thereabouts, because we needed to come back and we were going on foot or on bicycles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During these visits did you go into the camp or did you wait outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time when I went in that period between the 14th and 21st, at that time the camp was fenced in and you had to give the ID at the headquarters where the cafe used to be. You would pick it up again after you came out. The second time, yes, the second time I had help when I looked for my husband. There was a young man who used to work in the store ware of ours. In fact you could not even cross that fence any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The third time did you go into the camp yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, yes, because there was a big crowd of people, 1500 to 2000 people at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then you yourself went to Trnopolje with your daughter and your brother's two children and stayed there from 27th September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the inmates were going on 1st October and my brother thought that I could leave with them or at least bring the children. I could not do either. So the house where I was staying some people moved in right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the purpose of you going there at the end of September was to see if you could get on one of the buses or coaches that were to take people away from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and simply I had no supplies left. I had nothing to live on, and I did not dare to go on the convoys that the Serbs organised. There were bloody convoys. I had three children on me and I did not dare embark on such a journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did others like you also take the same step of going to Trnopolje at about that time in September to try to get on a convoy out of the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that there were about 3,000 of us inmates remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this time that you were at Trnopolje, you would have been there at the same time as the Jakupovic family, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst you were there presumably you were waiting to get on a convoy so that, again, you could leave the area and leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, not later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst you were there during those two months, were you able to leave the camp at all? Did you go outside the camp and go elsewhere during the daytime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on two or three occasions to Prijedor to buy and we had to pay the person who was bringing the bread, and we would pay him so that he would take us behind, behind the tarpaulin like cattle and take us to Prijedor. Two or three times is when I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During these occasions that you were at the camp, you say you saw Dule Tadic very often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would have been not quite two months, almost two months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that with certainty it would have been 20 times that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have described him being dressed in a military or a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I remember well that he had his sleeves turned up on his shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that on each occasion, each of the 20 occasions he arrived with his sleeves rolled up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I know when I -- maybe once or twice I remember. Whether it was every time, I think that is too much to ask, for me to know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The police uniform you say that he wore, what kind of uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dark blue. It was camouflage uniform. Not wholly white. It was not just multi-coloured and blue, but also grey and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, it was what we would call a blue camouflage uniform, would that be right, blue being the predominant colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, blue. Yes, a blue camouflage uniform. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he have a hat at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Maybe sometimes, but as far as I recall he was always without one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how he arrived at the camp, how he travelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I was coming out very rarely. I rarely went to the gate, so I could not see how he arrived. But I would see him in the camp, either in the school building or if the weather was nice outside, when I was outside and he had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So there seem to have been occasions then when you were outside and not just in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that I did not -- but there was a fence. It was well-known. That all counted as the camp. Outside of the camp was when you got out past the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got the bread from the man who delivered bread to you, where did you get the bread from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Prijedor. He was bringing in bread and he was selling it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But whereabouts did you get the bread from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first he would come into the yard itself and then later there was a gate there farther down just for pedestrians and before the war there was a gate for vehicles. Then he would pull in in reverse and sometimes he would stop on the road itself. Then we would form a line and would get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The military uniform you said that you saw Dusko Tadic in, are you able to describe that for us, how that looked to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was an overall and it was grey and olive, drab. I think that that is what it was, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what we would call a green camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not camouflage, I did not say that. I think it was a green, olive green.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So just a single colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So then in these two months you saw him what would amount to every third day, something like that, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe even every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right, every other day, very, very frequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he was in his police uniform, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I never knew the purpose of his coming, but I knew that he did, he was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he directing traffic or on a checkpoint? What was he doing in his police uniform, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, he did not -- there was no traffic there. There was no checkpoint. The checkpoints were around the camp and he was inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But without any particular purpose, so far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but again I do not believe that he would just come in for nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he was in his military uniform what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the first time when he came he came to look for Adil Jakupovic and his family. The second time when the inmates were leaving on 1st October, that may have been a period of two days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So these are two occasions that you can specifically tell us that he was doing something in particular, seeing ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- seeing Adil Jakupovic and being there when the convoy of buses was leaving Trnopolje which would have been, what, 1st or 2nd October after you had been there a few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those other -- well, if I may ask you first of all about when he came to see Adil Jakupovic. Did you see him then or was it because Nasiha or Adil had told you that Dusko Tadic had seen Adil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him in person myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we never talked. Before the war we did not even greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, because we lived maybe 150 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you related to the police chief in Prijedor, former police chief, a man called Tulundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In fact I do not even know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the other occasions that you saw Dusko Tadic, did you just see him outside in the camp or in any of the buildings of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both in the school building and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again now thinking about it a few years later, can you think of anything in particular that he was doing on any of those other visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall. I think that for me at that time it was something normal. Simply I was used to seeing this man there every other day. So I was not paying any particular attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the school building, where would you have been when you saw him at the school? Would you have been inside the building yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the building, because there were about 3,000 of us and there were only two bathrooms. So since the very morning there may be 200 to 300 people lining up and it went on until the night. There was a staircase maybe 10 metres, so he had to pass right there to go upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The school building was a place where a number of the people were held. It was full of women and children, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the school building have any administration within it for the camp or any other rooms relating to the running of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So these every other days that you were seeing him then inside the school building, it seems as though he was visiting people there? No other reason for him to be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know. I know on that occasion that he came to visit Adil and Nasiha and later I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are no other buildings connected with any or rooms connected with the running of the camp inside the school. It just held women and children and some men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were also a lot of men and after the inmates left, before they left there were a lot of inmates and there were tents that those poor people somehow made from blankets and plastic foil, and when they left there were 1500, 1600 people. Then there were people in the dom, a lot of people there, and in the school building. That is another school building, not the dom part of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt my friend, but there were three redactions which I thought I should attend to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want to finish where you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am just about to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we have time for redactions or should we do them now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They may have been attended to, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The places, yes, they have been. Excuse me, Mr. Kay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thought I would be able to finish it. It may be the case that I cannot, your Honour. What I will do is I will put my case to this witness at this stage and then continue after the luncheon adjournment. (To the witness): What I suggest to you is that you have made up all these visits to Trnopolje at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no need to make up things. I can only omit something because there was so much of it that I cannot even recall all of it, but not make up or add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, because you are so unhappy about the experiences to you Dusko Tadic is someone who gives you an opportunity to make allegations against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I have nothing against that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. May we request a redaction formally? I understand it has been attended to but, for the record, at points 12.20.14, 12.21.46 and 12.22.18.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand the redaction machine has speeded up so we may move a little quicker, if necessary, in the course of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May make the request within a shorter period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. We need to do that. 15 minutes -- is that a goal? OK, 15 minutes. Very good. Ask the witness to come in, please. ADVIJA CAMPARA, recalled. Cross-examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were at Trnopolje, were you in the same part of the school building as Nasiha Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was on the ground floor and Nasiha was on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were both in the same building, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, you were asked some questions about giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor previous to you coming to Court. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor's representatives, investigators, visited your home in October 1994, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it is exactly in October, but I know that it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When there took a statement from your husband ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- and did they take a statement from you at all when they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, when you were in the camp at Trnopolje in the period of time that you were there, did you either see or hear of anyone being mistreated or taken away from the camp and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evenings it could happen and that usually happened in the hall in the school building. That was on the ground floor. They would be taking out men, sometimes even women, but at that time they were mostly asking for money.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know what happened to these people that were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, they would be beaten up. At that time they knew that the inmates were not there, and most of those people which had to go with inmates had the money, and later on they had to give them a sum of money they were asking for. Sometimes they did not have the exact sum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I rise to my feet again, your Honour, as I fail again to see how this arises from cross-examination and, furthermore, what it has to do with the Prosecution rebuttal of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, during the course of the cross-examination, Mr. Kay questioned the witness particularly about the visits by Mr. Tadic and said, among other things, suggested, that there was no other reason but an innocent purpose of visiting people for him coming into the camp. In our submission, there could well be other explanations as to why people were coming into the camp other than an innocent explanation of simply visiting people. It is in relation to that that these questions are directed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, could the witness take her headphones off?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness, would you take your headphones off, please, Mrs. Campara?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again I do not ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We did not ask the witness if she speaks English, but anyway .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, I fail to see how this is a rebuttal of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even if it is not a rebuttal of the Defence case, is it covered by cross? Because, even if it is not a part of the rebuttal, if it is covered by cross, then that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not and it fails any test of relevancy that I am aware of because what this witness is saying is nothing to do with Mr. Tadic at all, the fact that other people may visit Trnopolje, the fact that she may hear that other people have had money taken from them. We are concerned with Mr. Tadic's case here. If the Prosecution are going to go on this line of opening all of the issues in the case, we are going to get a stage where the trial will never end.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule the objection. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see these events happen yourself -- madam, did you see these events with people being taken out yourself? Was this something you observed yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people being taken out, were they taken out by the guards or by the people who visited the camp or a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not to be seen. It was very dark. There was no electricity. It all happened very late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from what you tell us then, madam, the occasions when you cited Dusko Tadic at Trnopolje were not at night visiting people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not know whether he was visiting at night. I saw him during the day because at night you could not see anybody's face and recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, I had not understood before what the feeding arrangements were at Trnopolje. I rather gather that there was no kitchen and no food supplied for the inmates, is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning maybe for about a week when the inmates left, we were receiving food from the International Red Cross. These were one-day packets of food. After that they stopped taking that food. They were bringing in flour, but we did not get any flour, the Serbs got it, and we for about a week got a quarter of a bread loaf, and after that that was abolished and we had to pay for the bread and there was no kitchen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Campara, you are free to leave. You are permanently excused. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mrs. Munevera Kulasic. MRS. MUNEVERA KULASIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Kulasic, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, your name is Munevera Kulasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Prijedor and I lived there up until the 9th October, apart from a four year period, four years and some two months, whilst I was a student in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you study when you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an economist. That means that I studied at the Economic Faculty in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Before the war did you work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked since 1965 for some 14 years in the mining complex in Ljubija and after that in the Commercial Bank up until -- since 1980 till 20th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you live in your own apartment before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was that apartment owned by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mining complex, Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an apartment located at Pecani, building B, entrance No. 2 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Pecani, in that building, lived my sister with her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was your sister married to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her husband's name is Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Hasan Talundzic and your sister leave that apartment in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first the wife, then the children and he left later on in May, somewhere in mid May or at the end of May. I do not know the exact date. I think it was at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did Hasan Talundzic have when he left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the takeover by the Serbs, he was the head of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did someone else in your family move into that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I should explain to you that at that time we were considering that maybe the apartment could be kept in case somebody would be living in there, as on the 30th May the old town, this part of Prijedor which is called the old town, so on 30th May in the evening, on 30th to 31st May, that part of town, people were moved out of it and a good deal of it was even destroyed. My mother's sister, that is my aunt, that used to live in the old town and did not have any place to live then, and also her son's house was destroyed, the son's house which was somewhere else. Then what we did was that she would go in that apartment which belonged to my sister and Hasan Talundzic. So that was maybe on 3rd, 4th or 5th June. I cannot remember the exact date. Another one of my sisters registered her with a particular police department which was concerned with this particular street in Pecani, because whoever lived in a different part of town or started to live in a different part of town had to get registered. So, we put her in that flat and in order for her not to be alone, my mother went there with another of our sisters and so there were three of them in that particular apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How many sisters do you have altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have five sisters and a brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that the apartment belonged to your sister and Hasan Talundzic. Who actually owned the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mining complex, Ljubija. Maybe I should explain to you, the mining complex, Ljubija, it is a very big company that had a large number of apartments. Just before the war, there were some 5,000 employees there in the mining complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they have a number of apartments in that particular building, the mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that building and elsewhere in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any people monitoring or acting as security at the entrance to that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only in that building, but in all the buildings -- that was in June, after 30th May when that attack on Prijedor happened as it was described, that is, since that crisis situation -- in all the apartment buildings there were guards, not really guards, people who used to live in those houses, those buildings. They were there monitoring who was going into the building, who he was visiting and when that person was leaving. That was supposed to be done for all the people who were not residents in a particular building. So, that was also true for that particular building and it was registered who was going in and out. I know that because I used to visit my mother and every time that I would go in I was registered, and they would ask me who I was going to visit and they would also record the time when I would be going out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the Ljubija mine company recording who was living in the apartments which it owned in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at first, because somewhere from mid June onwards there was some kind of a committee formed by the mining company and they were going around these apartments to check whether the people who were there were those who used to live there before, and who actually had these particular apartments allocated to them, because at that time one way or the other some people had left the apartments where they used to live before the war. That particular committee made a register of who was actually living in their apartments, whether rightfully or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe this apartment? How big was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite a big apartment. We had two bedrooms and I think it had a bit more than 80 square metres, between 80 and 90 square metres. A two bedroom apartment and a living room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position had Hasan Talundzic had in order to be able to get this apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic was an engineer, an electricity engineer, at the time when he got his first one bedroom apartment as an expert working in a particular company. From that one bedroom apartment he moved into this two bedroom apartment, I think, for some two years before the beginning of the war. He also had three children of different -- both boys and girl, different sex, and when the committee was allocating apartments he was allocated a bigger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this apartment considered to be a large apartment in terms of the other apartments that are available in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because some two or three years, maybe even longer, before that, a decision was made that no three bedroom apartments would be built. So that was a couple of years before the beginning of the war when the larger than two bedrooms apartments stopped being built in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you had visited your sister while she lived there. Did you also help your sister decorate this apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a way I felt the obligation to do so. I was the second child out of seven children that my parents had and all my life I tried to help my family. So I also helped them whilst they were moving from the smaller into this larger apartment, and I have obviously visited them very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time that your sister and her husband left the area and the other members of your family moved in, was the apartment fully furnished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was fully furnished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe some of the details of the furnishings that were in that apartment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I can do that very easily, but before that, I do not know whether you are aware of it, but Bosnian Muslims in general give extreme -- pay very much attention to the apartments because they do spend quite a lot of time in their apartments, depending on their financial situation. It depends how they are going to decorate it and furnish it. As my sister and her husband had a very high standard, maybe more than the average, then they decorated this flat very, very nicely. As an example, I can describe the largest room in the apartment. It is a living room. Those were apartments that later on were sort of decorated in a more modern way, so the dining area was in the same room as the living room. So there were no separations and it was quite large, eight by four metres, and there was a separate kitchen where food was prepared. That room, I said there were two parts of the room. In the upper part towards the windows, there was a hand woven carpet. There was also a sofa and there were hand woven curtains on the windows. In the other part where there was a dining table there was a dark blue carpet. So I hope that you could have an idea of what the room -- how the room was furnished. There was obviously a stereo there and there was a chest of drawers, and there were also some plants that went very high up to the ceiling. They used to have those plants for some seven or eight years was the time that it took for those plants to grow so up high. There were also some large Chinese vases there. It was a very nice living area. The other part of the apartment was also furnished. My sister's bedroom had all the necessary, necessary furniture in there with all the carpets. The beds -- and the carpets were also woven. In the third room which they used to call the children's room, that room was quite large. There was even a possibility to separate it in two smaller rooms. They thought maybe of doing it because they had two girls and a boy because that room had two windows and two doors. That was particularly built in that way in order for people to have this possibility to separate it into two rooms. There was a sofa bed which was dark blue and there was another bed where the girls were sleeping. There was this time a normal, a carpet, industrial type of carpet, on the floor. The kitchen was normally furnished with all the necessary appliances. There was the fridge, the cooker and all the necessary crockery and cutlery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did your sister and a husband have a television set in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, there was no TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they have other valuables such as silver sets and handmade embroidery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was also a embroidered table cloths and they had a silver set of -- it was a big tray maybe half a metre long, maybe even longer, by 35 centimetres maybe, with implements for sugar, for coffee and it was non-standard. He inherited it from his mother who got it from his son who lives in Canada. I know that it was worth, I just happen to know it was worth about 3,000 Canadian dollars. They also had a crystal objects, unique objects. There were vases and glassware and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On about 20th June 1992, were you staying in that apartment with your mother and your aunt and your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. It was not approximately. It was exactly on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all who are present here probably remember when you started working the first day on a job, and one is even likely to remember the last day on a job. That was the last day of my work, and after I finished my day I went to my mother's and stayed there the night. She was not feeling too well. So I found myself there the next day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened on the morning of 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning I did what I usually do. I went and bought bread and milk and very soon after my return two policemen came. That was the civilian police, that is, the police force that was called "militia" at that time. So two of them came and one of them entered the room and the other one stayed in the hallway. He explained -- first, he asked who lived there, who and what they were and the other one was inspecting the apartment. I was -- I do not know what he was looking for. I did not accompany him there, but the gentleman who came into the living room for a while sat at this table and I sat across from him. He said that my mother could not be in that apartment, that the man whose apartment it was was not there and so that they would have to leave. For a while I discussed this with him, trying to explain that this was my sister's apartment and why. However, this conversation, I do not know how long it went on, but not too long, this man left after that. But at that time he did not insist that we leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said these two men were civilian police. Can you describe the uniforms that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The one who stayed in the hallway, I cannot say exactly, but the one who went -- came into the room, he had a light blue shirt and darker blue pants. That was the civilian police uniform at the time. I know that he was wearing a shirt only at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they search through the apartment while they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman who talked to me did not and I think that the other one did go round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After these policemen left, did some other men arrive at your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that may have been after about half an hour to an hour, two gentlemen arrived, one of whom I know very well and they both introduced themselves. They said that they were from the commission for apartments for the Ljubija mining company, that they were making -- that they were checking to see whether people who had the leases on these apartments actually lived in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did these men do while they were in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again they came to the living area. They sat down at the table and one of them, actually both of them, had maps, like ledgers -- I do not know how you call them -- in which they entered notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were your mother and sister doing while these men were in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister was sitting and my mother was lying down. That day my mother was not feeling too well. So she was still in her morning clothes and she was lying on the couch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While these men were in your apartment did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those men were in the apartment. One was sitting across from me and one next to me and I was facing one, the one -- the gentleman, his name is Boro Simic and he was a civil engineer at the Ljubija mining company. They started writing down the basic data about the apartment, and at that moment, as far as I could see, two men in uniforms entered the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know either of these men when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two that entered, no, I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did these men do who came into your apartment in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they walked in, I had an impression that they were surprised to have found these other two men in the house. One of them addressed the two men asking, "What are you two doing here? Who are you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the men from the Ljubija mine committee explain what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic introduced both of them and told them the reason why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the men in uniform say to the men from the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the two in uniforms said that they had no business being there, and he told them to leave the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men from Ljubija tried to explain again, and the other one would not allow him that and he ordered him to leave, that they had no business in that apartment any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later learn the identity of this man in uniform who was talking to the men from the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For one, yes, for the other one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the name of the man who was doing the talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How was Dusko Tadic dressed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a camouflage uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the primary colour of that camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is green and brown, you know, like the camouflage military uniform that the military wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the other man who was with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw one of them because he entered the room. Whether there were others outside or in other rooms -- my mother says that there were another two of them but I never saw them. So the other one had the olive green pants and black t-shirt, and black gloves with no fingers. At that time, at least our impression at that time, was that it was an image of a sniper, whether -- that the snipers wore such outfits but I do not know if that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What colour hair did this other man have, the one with the black t-shirt and the olive green pants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a young man rather lanky, brown hair, rather light, somewhat pale complexion with a small, not very full, beard like this and that is what he wore it. The remainder of the face was clean shaven. It was just down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, the gesture the witness made appeared to be under the chin coming to a point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Once Borislav or Boro Simic and the other man left, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object to this evidence which I have allowed to take it as far as it has, and it goes to the whole purpose of rebuttal evidence in this trial. From what we have heard so far, there is no reason why the Prosecution could not have called this evidence as part of its main case. When L ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful for your Honour noticing that. Could the witness remove the headphones, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please take off your headphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What the Court should be hearing now is evidence that would not have been reasonably anticipated in the presentation of the Prosecution case. When the Defence sought to recall L for further cross-examination, the stipulation of the Court was that we were only allowed to raise issues that we could not have reasonably foreseen when cross-examining him on the first occasion that we did so. We advised the Court appropriately of the issues we were to deal with. In relation to this evidence, the Court was aware from the presentation of the Prosecution case that as part of their profile against the defendant on a number of occasions they referred to the flat in Pecani and its previous occupation by Mr. Talundzic, as the head of the SUP, as being something that was provided for him and, in those circumstances, something, because of his position, would only have been provided for him. In relation to the evidence that we are hearing now, this material should have formed part of the original Prosecution case. It is not material that is arrived at at a later stage to rebut issues exclusively raised by the Defence, to rebut issues in relation to the case by which the Prosecution are taken by surprise; far from it. This forms part of the major framework of their case and, from the evidence that we have heard, there is no indication why this evidence has to be called after the Defence has closed its case. It seems to me that the purpose of rebuttal evidence may be being used by the Prosecution to have what we could call as a second bite of the cherry to reconstruct the case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or "apple" -- I thought you were going to say "apple".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It is an apple where we come from.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Some places "apples", others whatever, plums perhaps. We have heard a lot about that. Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In fact, I think my friend misjudges part, in fact the majority, as I would submit, of the purpose of rebuttal, and that is to rebut the evidence brought forward by the Defence if they so choose. In fact, the accused and his wife testify in great deal about how they came about, how they came to receive this apartment and then the circumstances under which the transfer of the apartment was made. This evidence is going to rebut that particular story.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule your objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You need to put your headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Miss Kulasic, the last question I asked was after the men from the Ljubija mining company left, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Dusko Tadic told us that we had to leave the apartment. I tried to explain that this was my mother, that this was the apartment of her daughter, but he said, "Let her go to her apartment. She has nothing to do here", and that we had to leave the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In what tone was he addressing you? How was he speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in a rather raised voice, rather like giving an order to which you could not object. You could try to talk, but it was basically an ordering tone of the voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you try to explain to him that it was your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I explained that it was the apartment of my sister's, that it was theirs and he said, "No, they are not there any more, so it is not their apartment any more".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you manage to sit down and try to fill out some paperwork with respect to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was sitting at that table, as I -- and I told you where I was sitting and then I said, "All right, the apartment belongs to the Ljubija mining complex, but the things in it, the property, belongs to my sister and her husband. They bought it." He said, "OK, we will make an inventory of it".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who wrote out this inventory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took a piece of paper and wrote: "A complete bedroom, a fully furnished living room, fully finished -- a kitchen" without any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then what did he do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He signed that piece of paper. He gave it to me. I signed it too, and when I tried to take it he said, "Oh, no, you don't need this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the name that was signed to the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko, Dusko Tadic, Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this time what were your mother and your sister doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While he was writing this down, this inventory, I was trying to convince my mother that she should get up and get dressed so that we can get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic make any comments about the belongings when you explained about the belongings to him, the possessions in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he said, "Here, we all wrote it all down and then this will be decided on. We put together a report". But if that was a whole inventory report, then I should have had it and he said, "No, you don't need it". Then after that I said, "Well, in that house there are also books, children's books. It is something that is theirs. They need it, their toys", and he said, "No, those children will not need these things. They will not be coming back here. They will never need it again". That is how he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Once the inventory was done, what did Dusko Tadic say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, then he said, "It is over. You have to go." So he hurried us so that we would leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say he "hurried" you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we had to leave fast, this apartment, that we had to leave the apartment, that we could not be there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he give you time to pack your clothes and other things that you wanted to take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We took it very hastily. My mother collected her things and then I said, "Well, give me those things". She had some of her personal things because she had been staying there for about 15 days by then. So there were a few belongings of the aunt, and she hastily collected those things and I took my clothing. At the time I had a jogging suit on and after I changed from work, and so we took it out in front of the apartment to the staircase in our arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How old is your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother is now exactly 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this time were you, your mother and sister afraid for your safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Every time somebody in a uniform came to the apartment caused fear to the person in whose apartment they were entering. That was already the atmosphere there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately, how long from the time that Dusko Tadic first came into your apartment was it before you were forced out the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was about 15 minutes, I do not know exactly, but it was a very short period of time, however long it took when I talked to them, and let us call that a report was written, and then my mother collecting her belongings and then we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The belongings that you managed to collect, you were able to carry out in your arms out to the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except that I also took out two vases which I could not take with me when we went back to our house. So I left it with a neighbour so that I would collect them later. That is all -- all that I took of the possessions in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was Dusko Tadic armed during the time that he was in the apartment? Did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
