utterances.text: Yes, but that was the time when people in uniform, I never saw anybody who did not have -- who did not carry weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were out in the hall what did you see happen next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we left the apartment, the civilian policeman that I mentioned before, he had just arrived again, and as he looked through the door towards the living area he was now surprised too a little bit to see those other people there, and Dusko turned to him and he said, "What are you looking here? You have no business there". So that person left, that civilian policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then what happened out in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we left the apartment, we were the first ones to leave and after that the two of them left, Dusko Tadic. That is the moment when I learned his name. He changed the lock on the door and put a note on the door where it read "Dusko Tadic". That is when I read it and then I learned his real name because I could not very well see the signature on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there anything else on the paper besides the name "Dusko Tadic" that was put on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was also a number, I cannot remember the number exactly. I think it was something like "BP" and a number. I think that was a record number of some unit, a military unit. They used to put some kind of particular record numbers in the -- when the military would be moving into particular apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later call the apartment to try to get your sister's belongings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who did you speak to the first time you called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I called that apartment on Monday morning, I went to the police station to report what had happened, still believing that the police was in charge of the order in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to get any help at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I explained what apartment it was and to whom it belonged, the man I talked to looked at me in surprise. He called somebody on the phone and told me to wait outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were waiting what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whilst I was waiting outside in the hallway of the police station, I saw that from the opposite door, the door opposite to the entrance of the police station, a man in a uniform was taking a civilian, a citizen of Prijedor whom I knew very well and of whom I had earlier heard he was in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When that man was taken out of the building I was at that moment thinking, I have already said whose apartment that was. The husband of my sister was not in town any more. Nobody knew where he was. I became scared and I left the SUP building. I simply left. I did not wait for them to call me back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then did you later call the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I think about a day or two later, I phoned the apartment of my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I asked whether Dusko was there. A female voice answered the phone. At first, the first time round I think that was a voice of an older woman and she said Dusko was not there. I called again, I cannot remember whether the same day or the day after, and then a younger female voice answered the phone and I realised this was Dusan Tadic's wife. I talked to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask to retrieve the property of your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I introduced myself. I said I was the sister of the woman to whom the apartment belonged. I asked when I could get their belongings that were in the apartment. Then that woman in a very astonished voice said, "And what do you think you should get?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you make any arrangements with that woman to get the property of your sister back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "I think that I should get everything that is in the apartment which is privately owned by my sister".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did she respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did not say anything to me then. The next time I phoned I talked to Dusko. I asked when he would be at home. She told me that, and the next telephone call I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This response, you said, in a voice of astonishment, "What do you think you should get?" how did you take that answer? What did you think she meant by that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was astonished that I was asking for anything, where did I get the right to ask for anything from that apartment? That is why she said, "What do you think you should get? Where do you have the right to ask for anything?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later talk to Dusko Tadic on the phone about your sister's property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to him. He told me that his wife had told him about my telephone call and he said, "OK". He asked me where I lived. I told him where I lived, where my apartment was, and he said that he will bring the things to me. Nobody said what or when. He simply said that he will bring those things to the place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later see Dusko Tadic? Did he show up at your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day when he told that he would bring the things, he came with another man. They rang my door bell and we discussed, we talked then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he say? What did Dusko Tadic say? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic said that he had brought that man so that they could see exactly where I lived, and that that man will bring all the things to me on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The following day were some things delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day that man, which had been there with Dusko, brought on a cart driven by horses various things. This cart was a completely flat one, there was no guard rail on them. On that cart there were some seven or eight huge bundles of wardrobe, and on that cart there were also small boxes, cardboard boxes, in one some toys, and in the other some old crockery. Also there was a small bag with crystal pieces, and when the cart pulled up in the courtyard and the bag fell on the concrete floor, and there was this awful noise of the glass breaking when falling on the concrete floor. Later on when I saw it, everything was broken, all that glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The six or seven bundles, they contained clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it contain all of the clothing from the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, these were mostly children's clothes, and maybe also selected less valuable wardrobe belonging to my sister and her husband. I remember, if it is important, that the suits -- a brand new suit my brother-in-law had never worn was not brought. Also, sort of a military suit was never brought. My sister had a leather suit and also a good jacket. Those things were not there. Those -- there were less good items that were brought from the Adil's wardrobe and the rest belonged to the children, and bundles were formed with sheets and there was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The silver service, that was not in the items that were brought to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The embroidery, the hand made embroidery, or the hand made curtains, were they brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dusko Tadic on another occasion after this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I saw Dusko with his wife on one occasion in the town. They were passing by further away. I saw him with a woman. I did not know at the time it was his wife, but when I saw her in the autumn she was wearing my jacket. I could recognise that jacket. It was a unique piece of clothing. As that woman was wearing it, I decided it was his wife. I saw Dusko on several other occasions from the window of the building where I used to live, that is, from the window of my mother's apartment that was partly overlooking the main street where the building was and he used to walk by in that street. The other part of my mother's apartment was overlooking the courtyard and people were also passing there in order to go to Pecani. I also saw him twice passing through that courtyard, but we never had personal contact afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The jacket that you saw that you recognised, you had left that in your sister's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the apartment. I did not leave it there. That jacket is very characteristic. It was a suit that was unique which I bought. That is why I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told the Court that Hasan Talundzic was the Chief of Police in Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One thing that is not clear to me is why he was in an apartment that belonged to the Ljubija mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic spent just about a year as the Chief of the Police, '91, '92. He was on that -- held that office for about a year, and before that all the time since 1975, he had worked in the Ljubija mining company. His wife had also worked for the mining company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So he was a professional engineer who worked for the Ljubija mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he worked for the Ljubija mining company, was he a policeman as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He had been the Chief of the Police for one year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking. After the elections in 1990/1991, then he was appointed. I think somewhere in early '91 he was appointed Chief of the Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say this happened, he had previously been an engineer and then, as a result of one of the parties winning the political elections, they appointed him to be Chief of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is, he was not -- did not only used to be, he is still an electrical engineer, and from 1975 till 1991 he worked as an engineer and then he was appointed the Chief of the Police. He was also a reserve first class captain. So he partly knew that type of duty. So that might have been one of the reasons why he was appointed head of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He had been a captain who was a reserve police officer, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, for the military because when he was doing his military service he was in the school for reserve officers and that is why he was a reserve JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But he was not a reserve police officer before he was made Chief of the Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His first appointment then to the police station at Prijedor was as Chief of the Police in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it one of the political parties who appointed him as Chief of the Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Party of Democratic Action had proposed him for the office, but at that time, according to the agreement made by the SDA and the SDS Parties, the SDA proposed a person who would be the head of the SUP, that is, the Chief of the Police and he was appointed after their proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He no longer worked for the Ljubija mining company when he was Chief of Police in Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he in any way supposed to move then to a police house, a house connected with the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. You mean for living there or for working? I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For living there, was he entitled or should he have moved to a house that was owned by the police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. According to the regulations which were valid at the time, after a certain number of years a person spent with a company or at least a number of years in a particular apartment, one person had what used to be called the right, a tenant's right. That is why Hasan Talundzic could keep the apartment, just as I, who left the mining company in order to go and work in a bank, could keep the tenant's right and the apartment that belonged to the mining company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the men from the Ljubija mining company came to the flat and your mother was there with your sister, is that right ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- the men from the Ljubija mining company, had they come to take the flat back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That commission was touring all the apartments in the town, and they were recording who was living in these apartments. So, they also came to that particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they mention anything about the fact that Hasan Talundzic, who had previously owned the apartment, was no longer living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not even have time to say that, because very soon afterwards Dusko came with another man and up until that point they managed to explain who they were, and saying that they were recording who lived in the mining company apartments. They did not have time to say anything else because they were obliged to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they say why they were recording who was living in the mining company apartments, what the purpose of doing that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only said that they were recording who was living in and making a register of who was living in their company's apartments. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your sister have any right to live there under the agreement with the Ljubija mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- which sister, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The sister who was in the flat with your mother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We thought it was normal because this was an apartment which was used by my sister and her husband. So she and my mother could have the right to be there because the apartment was not considered as an abandoned one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All I wanted to know was what the agreement was, whether that was possible under the arrangements with the Ljubija mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how things would have developed had we not been expelled from that particular apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time there were a number of commissions investigating who was living in property in Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was a commission that was made by the person who -- by the actual owner who constructed these apartments. The same commission was also checking who was living in my apartment, but there was no other commission that was going into the Ljubija mining company apartments. It was only the commission of the Ljubija mining company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to take instructions. That would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean, you would like to take instructions? You would like an opportunity to confer with counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Expressing it a different way, that is probably what I would say. I was expressing it in my own language.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, that is OK. I was just wondering whether it had anything to do with the timing. We can talk about it when we end today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you spoke to Dusko Tadic in relation to the house of your brother-in-law, he accepted that he was Dusko Tadic and that you were dealing with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. I -- as soon as we left the apartment he wrote "Dusko Tadic". When I talk on the phone, I asked for him and he answered and I talked to him. Then he arrived at my door of my apartment and we talked then again. So I had no dilemma about who that man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, in the apartment itself when you first met him he introduced himself to you as Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not say what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When your sister moved out of the house, the flat, where did she go to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did not move out. She only left Prijedor with her children, but she did not move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: She moved, you say she left Prijedor with her children. All I want to know is, where was she living? She moved away from the flat to live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When she left Prijedor to go and live in Croatia, did she take things with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She only took one bag and her three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can put the question this way, were further goods taken from the flat and sent to them after she had left by members of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. First of all, even if those things -- if anybody had taken anything because they could not have sent it to them because there was already fighting, the war, so it was impossible to send anything and, besides, my sister did not leave in order not to come back. She just took the children with her because of the situation. It was well-known what the situation was. So she was trying to rescue the children and not move out. Moving out was not her intention. We all thought at that time that it would -- this would last a month or two and everybody would go back to their homes. That is what we all thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When your aunt was in the flat, she was living there with your mother and another sister, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When they moved out of the flat, they went to live where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother returned to her apartment and I was already in my own -- living in my own apartment. The aunt came to live with my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, presumably, when your aunt went to live with your mother, that was in your mother's own flat where she had previously been living before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a large flat or a small flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother had a large apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your sister, did she return to live with her family then in the place where she had always lived before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the sister who was there at the time when my mother had to leave the apartment? Is that the sister you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that sister was to be with my mother all the time. In fact, I did not mention she had a meningitis case as a small child and was partially retarded, and so she was not able to live on her own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The goods that were delivered from the flat on the cart, were they delivered at your flat or at your sister's flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I do not know exactly what sister, which sister you have in mind. In that part of the building where my mother lived I had my own apartment in the same building and also my mother had her own apartment in that very same building, and let me explain. On the site where this apartment building was built, it was built on the site where our old family house used to stand. So my mother got an equivalent apartment, equivalent to the square area of the house which she used to have, which was about 110 metres. Now, that may not have been a perfect match to the square area, but that was the largest apartment they had in the building so they offered it to her when they tore down her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because at one stage before they left the flat, as I understand it, it was your aunt, your mother and your sister who were living in the flat of Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after 30th May when part -- the section of Prijedor was destroyed where my mother -- my sister lived, then my aunt, where my aunt used to live, then after this was destroyed she moved to the apartment where Hasan Talundzic used to live and she moved in there together with my mother and my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The place where your sister then went to live, having moved out of that apartment in Pecani, presumably, was already furnished? It already had goods within that flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The place where your sister went to live, having given up the flat to Dusko Tadic, and your aunt had to live, having given up the flat to Dusko Tadic, those places were already furnished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where my sister, my mother and myself at that time, we did not leave the apartment in order to give it over to Dusko Tadic. We were literally kicked out of that apartment. Before that my mother had her own apartment which she got from the Ljubija mining company as compensation for the house that was torn down. She lived in there with the sister and another sister and the brother and she returned to that apartment. Obviously, the aunt followed there. The sister whose apartment it was, the wife of Hasan Talundzic, went with a bag and her three children and she was in refugee facilities, I do not know what, in Croatia. Later she moved on and went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will use your language. The apartment that your sister, your aunt and your mother were kicked out of, where they then went to live were already furnished apartments, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the mother went back to her own apartment. Obviously, she had a furnished apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, there was a problem to store things such as the table and cupboards that were in the apartment that had belonged to Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no problem of that kind. I had my own garage in Prijedor which was empty and my brother, on the eve of the war, had also bought a business space which was also empty where a lot more furniture could have been stored than the amount of furniture that was in that apartment. So there was space for those possessions, had I received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you the only person who was talking to Dusko Tadic, or did your sister also speak to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister could not talk to him. As I said, she is partially mentally handicapped after she had meningitis as a young child, but my mother and I remember very well. She said -- my sister had just made some food and she said, "Let her finish the food" to which he said angrily that she would -- would she want to just fly out of the window?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because what I suggest to you is this, that some of the furniture could not be taken from that flat because there was a problem in storing it, and the clothes were something that could be taken from the flat and that you agreed should be delivered to you as Mr. Tadic arranged and did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I requested the things that were in the apartments. As I said, I only received bundles with clothing and, again I repeat, we had two spaces. I had an empty garage and my brother's business space. It is very easy to dismantle the furniture and send it there because when I had to leave my apartment, I disassembled and dismantled all of my furniture and moved it, some to my mother's apartment and some to the garage. So there was space available for the possessions from my sister's apartment, but I was not given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say you saw Mira Tadic wearing a jacket that belonged to you, did it not fit her properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a jacket that was part of a set. It was knee length and I recognised it. Maybe it is not important, but it was a unique piece of clothing and it was an exhibit at a fair and that is what I was told by the lady who sold it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just one, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect to your brother-in-law's apartment and the issue of the ownership of that apartment, your brother-in-law, Hasan Talundzic, and your sister still had the right to return to that apartment at the time you were kicked out of it, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, had my sister been in Prijedor, she would normally go into the apartment and live there unless somebody else in the uniform would come in and kick her out; otherwise nobody would move her from that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did your sister and brother-in-law leave Prijedor out of fear for the safety of their family and themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister left with her children precisely because of that reason and there were other women who left at that time, but she had an additional reason which was her husband's position in the city at the time. He was still in Prijedor but not in his apartment. He was -- he did not dare be there. I could maybe relate a detail here: all Muslims who were earlier in the TO or had military uniforms as reserve personnel had to turn it in, return it to the military, and in my sister's apartment there was a military uniform and a military book and everybody who would come to the apartment, because earlier other people showed up to search and they were all looking over this military uniform, but they were all leaving it there. I can only assume they thought that he would come back. So it is interesting that the military uniform was never taken away from this apartment and the Muslims had to turn in all their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One question, witness, and it is what happened to Mr. Talundzic? Did he manage to escape from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Talundzic at that time was in Prijedor. I can say that now. He was at his sister's of whom most of those people did not know that it was his sister because she did not have the same last name. So he was staying with that sister of his. It is later -- it was later that I found out that at the end of July he managed to leave Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is all I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is alive. Thank God he is alive -- unlike the husband of my other sister's, a husband who remained in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Kulasic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Kulasic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also want to thank you for giving me an opportunity to say what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, much as been said in this trial about uniforms, SMB uniforms, olive green uniforms and so on. I was wondering whether you could provide us with pictures of the various types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We can go through the archives that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the next witness is Fikret Kadiric. FIKRET KADIRIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, your name is Fikret Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Rizvanovici, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you also raised in Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How large was your family, the family you grew up with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Father, mother and six children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many brothers, how many sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps anticipating a question, if I could have the witness shown Exhibit 280, perhaps we could have the witness indicate where Rizvanovici is -- you have found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Kadiric, where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elementary school I finished in Rizvanovici, then the secondary in Prijedor and education -- school for education of pedagogics in Zagreb, in Petrina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you trained as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently work as a teacher in Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After nine years as a teacher, did you change careers and join the police force in Prijedor in 1975?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to be exact, on 1st March 1975 I moved to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the time you joined the police department in opstina Prijedor, how many Muslims were member -- first of all, let me ask you, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the time you joined the police department in Prijedor in 1975 how many Muslim members of the police force were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that the ethnic structure was lopsided. It was 15 to 18 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you began in 1975, did you begin your career as an assistant to the Commander of the main Prijedor station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1977, did you become Commander of the police unit or branch in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1978, did you return to Prijedor again as an assistant to the Commander, this time in charge of the criminal department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1981 did you become acting Commander of the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1985 or early 1986, did you become Commander of the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the police station in Prijedor also have responsibility for the outlying units or branches in places like Kozarac and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadiric, in 1991 were the administrative positions of the police department redistributed in accordance with or in response to the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who took your position as Commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which Party had nominated him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know him as someone who was closely associated with SDS and its leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see him frequently in conference or together with leaders of the SDS Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially after he was appointed the Commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was appointed head of the SUP, the public security services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which Party appointed him or nominated him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you a member of either SDA or SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When Dusan Jankovic took your position as chief of the Prijedor police, what position were you moved to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a Commander of the traffic police unit by appointment from the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the national composition or ethnic composition of the traffic police at the time you became Commander of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again lopsided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy Commander of the traffic police when you became Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ziad Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he replaced by someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Ziad Basic the deputy Commander of the traffic police when you were Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Djuro Prpos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he work for the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a deputy Commander of the traffic police. He was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There maybe some confusion with the question. What was Ziad Basic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an assistant Commander of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that a position below deputy Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the assistant?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Which position was subordinate and which position was superior between the deputy Commander and the assistant Commander in the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- the hierarchy is the Commander, the deputy, the assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also know a man known as Zoran Cvijic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the traffic police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What part of the traffic police did he work in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to duty to the station, he was working at the desk. He had a desk job, an administrative job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any reason why Zoran Cvijic was working at a desk job rather than on patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently, he had been sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of illness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently, it was nerves. It was the nerves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of reputation did he have as a traffic police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not -- he did not have a great reputation. A lot of people -- his colleagues thought that he was faking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he in addition to the complaints of nerves, a nervous condition, was he trusted as someone who could be on patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was appointment or selection to the traffic police considered a desirable position or considered a desirable appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among them there was an opinion that this was a privileged position and so everybody who worked at the station, they all wanted to go into the traffic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it an easy or a difficult job to obtain? Did it require any effort or connections to obtain that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, what I could see from most who worked there, most of them got to get those duties through some connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that it was considered something of a privileged position and people wanted to get into traffic. In what way was it seen as privileged or attractive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the job was easier because you used a vehicle. The population that you worked with was an easier population to work with, motorists, and there were fewer, there was less risk, risk for one's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were traffic policemen regarded by members of the general population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had more respect from people than the regular policemen in the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that respect because people admired them or respect for another reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what way were members of the general public afraid of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not so much the general population, but the motorists, because a lot of people drove under influence and would know what sanctions there would be if they would be caught when under influence, or if he make any violations they could have their driver's licence revoked or some other similar sanctions, which for those people was very damaging, especially if they had to stop working and that was their only profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would the significance of the work performed or the responsibilities or role of the traffic police be increased or decreased during wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in the beginning, in the first period, their duties would be increased and then maybe later after all the events that took place, in my opinion, their duties and responsibilities would be diminishing more and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why would the role of the traffic police be increased at some point during wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because everything that was going -- everything that was happening was going by the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadiric, we have heard evidence in this Court that the takeover of opstina Prijedor and of the police department took place on the night of April 29th/the morning of April 30th. Do you recall where you were that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at my father's in his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was not your normal place of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Had you gone to your father's home at least in part because of threats or warnings which you had received that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the threats, did you receive them in person or over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was said to you? What was said to you over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An unknown voice phoned. They cursed my Ustasha mother saying, "We will come and get you. You will soon be liquidated".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the voice of the person who was making those threats either during that particular call or any subsequent calls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the second phone call I felt that I somehow knew that voice, I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who did you believe that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am convinced that that was the voice of a former policeman who was expelled from duties and his name was Ralic Radovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing at that time, what his work was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the so-called police. That was at the garrison of the JNA, in the barracks of the JNA, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were in Rizvanovici when the takeover occurred. How did you actually learn that the takeover had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of the 30th, around 5 o'clock in the morning, I heard hard knocks at the entrance door of my father's house. I cautiously left and looked through the door and I saw two policemen. I opened the door. I saw that they were scared and not even waiting for me to ask them what was going on, they told me that Prijedor had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were these policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did they say what had happened to the policemen of Prijedor, the Muslim policemen of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on duty that morning when the Serb police, armed and helped and supported by the Yugoslav Army, had disarmed all the policemen that were non-Serbs, that is Muslims and Croats, and they had sent them home. In other words, they were ordered to go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Muslim policemen who came to your door indicate to you whether you should or should not go to the police station that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they told me not to go, because I was looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you remain in the in Rizvanovici until ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- until after the attack on Hambarine on May 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that time did you then flee to the Pecani neighbourhood of Prijedor to your sister-in-law's home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My home was there, my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you arrested in Pecani on May 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who came to arrest you - civilians, military, police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the flat with my mother-in-law and three policemen rang the bell, three active duty policemen from the police station. A relative of mine opened the door and they asked him: "Is Fikret there?" He answered "Yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you came to the door did the policeman indicate that you were under arrest and should come with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were those policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did they transport you to the police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a military vehicle, a jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About what time of the day was this, morning, afternoon, evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the early afternoon, somewhere just after lunch time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the SUP do you know whether or not people there were aware of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you come to know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whilst getting off the vehicle I looked up towards the windows and I noticed that in almost every office there were my former colleagues watching my arrival, watching my arrival, and some of them were even laughing at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken, into what part of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first floor in the office of the previous Deputy Commander of the police station, Simo Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was someone left there to guard you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a retired police officer, Inspector Ilija Bijelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a window in that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to see outside through that window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point after your arrival did you see Muslim prisoners being brought to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a while, I do not know after how much time had past since I was brought there, I heard beatings, screamings, shoutings, shooting. After that the person who guarded me got up and went towards the window to watch what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also take that opportunity to get up and see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also got up, stood by him and was watching what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you see outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of the post office towards the SUP there was a tank going. On that tank there were two soldiers with hands raised, with three fingers raised, and they were shooting from the automatic rifles. After that I saw first one, then a second bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see prisoners get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the buses stopped just in front of the main entrance of the SUP, and two soldiers got off the bus. They got off the buses and they posted themselves just on the left and right-hand side of the bus doors. The people were running with their hands on the back of their heads. They were running towards the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were these people dressed, those who were running from the bus with their hands on the back of their heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a different way. There were people who had bare feet. There were people who did not have any top clothing or they had just shirts, under shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the nationality of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the buses arrived and the prisoners started to leave the bus, did you hear any sounds of movement in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard people running through the corridors of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Running in which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the hallway, the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So as the prisoners were coming towards the entrance of the SUP, people from inside the SUP were going down in the direction of the entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were running.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see any Serbian officials as the prisoners got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the SDS President, Simo Miskovic, who was standing in front of the Municipal Assembly building with an automatic rifle, a heckler, in his hands. Skondric Vaso was with him, he was a police inspector from Sarajevo, he also had a heckler rifle, and he was wearing a uniform, while Simo was dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the prisoners from the bus went toward the entrance and as the people from the SUP went down toward the entrance, did you hear any sounds coming from the area of the entrance of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could hear people swear, curse, shouting, screaming, screams.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kinds of curses did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Alija, fuck you, fuck your Ustasha mother", and those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kinds of screams did you hear? Were those the screams of people in pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were screams of people in pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Simo Miskovic and Vaso Skondric. From the time of your arrival until the arrival of these prisoners, had you become aware of other Serbian police officials or other officials in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were, almost all of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was there? Can you name some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, Dusan Jankovic, Milos Jankovic, Ranko Mijic, Djuro Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As you were held in the room you indicated, could you smell anything unusual in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whilst they were bringing me in, in the corridors there were scattered untidily cardboard boxes. There were also tins, then crates of beer and one could smell a stench of alcohol everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The cardboard boxes you mentioned, were those the kinds of boxes which held cans of beer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not cans of beer, cans of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the time the takeover took place did you receive indications that Serbian police officers were aware that it was about to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could feel it by the behaviour of certain policemen of Serb nationality that something was going on, that the duties were not carried out as they used to be previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any Serb police officer ever come to you and indicate to you that the arming of Serbs was taking place and that bad developments were about to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but it was shortly after I was appointed Commander of the police station. Zdravko Tobica, a policeman, came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did he tell you about arming or bad developments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that things that were going on were not good, that there was already a separation, a division between the policemen, and that their SDS was arming people that were living in Pecani where he lived and I lived, and that something should be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Serbs being armed. Was it among the duties of the traffic police to confiscate weapons deemed illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whilst on duty all the illegal weapons were to be seized during the control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During your time as a traffic police commander did you learn that any of your subordinates were interfering with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My deputy Djuro Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to deal with that interference without a direct confrontation with Djuro Prpos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, what was Prpos doing? Was he forbidding police officers, traffic police officers to confiscate the weapons or was he returning them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was returning them without my knowledge and without asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you learned about that did you give orders that weapons should not be returned without your direct orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you later learn that those weapons were simply no longer being confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In smaller quantities as compared to the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To which national group were the weapons that Prpos returned returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Djuro Prpos in contact with Serbian military leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there ever a confrontation between the Serb military and the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that involve an attempt by the traffic police to do their normal duty and search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was during the attempt by a traffic police patrol who tried to enter the Prijedor barracks. They were asked to accompany, escort some military vehicles. Then Radovan Rajlic, Stojan Madzar and some others stopped them, and they searched systematically the police vehicle, although they had no right to do so. Also they searched all the policemen who were on the patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was this a matter that you normally would have responded to as Commander of the traffic police and which you intended to deal with as traffic police Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to telephone one of the superior officers in the barracks. Then I did not succeed in this and I said that our policemen will not escort anybody any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that matter ultimately resolved by the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards my deputy, Djuro Prpos, received the Commander of that unit. His name was Rajlic and he used to work at the Post Office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Prpos and the Commander of that unit work out an arrangement on behalf of the traffic police without the Commander of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Serbian military continue to deal with Djuro Prpos and circumvent the Commander of the police, in this case you, in further dealings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that confrontation they decided not to contact the traffic police, but they contacted the general police station and its Commander Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In further dealings with the traffic police, however, did the Serbian military exclude you but deal with Prpos instead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and with Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the takeover did you receive information that Serbian police and Serbian leaders had been planning the takeover well in advance of its occurrence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was it you learned? How was that takeover being planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days after I returned from the camp I met in Zagreb with my wife. She had arrived from Prijedor, or it is better to say that she was forced to leave. Among other things, she told me that Milinko Sujica, a policeman who moved into my flat, while going away, while they were saying goodbye, said that whatever had happened had been planned a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he say where that planning took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Prijedor barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he say who participated in that planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the employees of the Serbian nationalities from the Prijedor SUP and that they had established a Serbian SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he indicate whether or not the Serbian employees of the SUP had been instructed to keep this planning secret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, he said that to my wife and that is precisely how things were. They were not allowed to say that to anybody, that was forbidden, and it was also dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadiric, I want to take you very briefly beyond the SUP just to let the Court know where you ended up after you were taken from there, but I want to ask you one more question before I did. You mentioned Zoran Cvijic before. Was he put in the administrative unit because he had particular administrative competence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was ill and that was temporary up until the moment a final decision would be taken as to his duty post. I actually found him working in that particular job at the police station when I came to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken from the SUP on the night of May 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around 10 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken to the SUP in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated over a period of time there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole night and the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the interrogators demand that you respond to certain questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kinds of things were they asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing they told me was that I was a Commander of the Green Berets, some kind of Muslim army, and that I have to tell them everything about that because they knew, allegedly, everything about me and my activities in that particular field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Over time what kinds of questions did they demand you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was the exercise, the training place, what kinds of weapons we had and where those weapons came from; who were the people working with me and who were my contacts in Sarajevo. He mentioned Avdo Hebib who was the Deputy or Assistant Minister at that time, how many times he came to see me and what instructions he had given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you provide the interrogators with the answers they appeared to want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I did not have anything to answer to what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you failed to give them the answers they were looking for, were you beaten and tortured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, till unconsciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kinds of instruments did they use as they beat and tortured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rubber bats, wooden poles, pistol, knife, wires.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On what parts of your body were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From top to toe, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the soles of your feet beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to put my feet on a chair, on the back of the chair they were so they could beat the soles of my feet, the palms of my hands, my back, on my hips, until I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of the interrogation and the torture, were there any indications that your interrogators were in contact with Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that based on the kinds of questions they were asking you and the information they came up with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first question which I had spoken of before, from that room where they had brought me Vlado Karan came out, and after several minutes he came back smiling, saying: "Oh, but you didn't say anything about your plans about establishing a camp for the Serbian population." He ordered me to say everything about it because he had information about it, even some lists that I had made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there such a plan to establish a camp for the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadiric, without going into all of the things that happened to you after you were taken to Dubica, did you eventually end up in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First in the hospital in Bosanska Gradiska, then in prison in Stara Gradiska and then in the camp in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your family, that is your father and mother and brothers and sisters, remain in Rizvanovici after your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you eventually learn what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that during the cleansing of the Hambarine area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of that complete area that is called Brdo, and the villages of Biscani, Rizvanovici, Rakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you learn what happened to other members of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time my younger brother was taken out of the house and killed as well as his son aged 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many members of your family were killed in the Hambarine area during the cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my family, smaller family 12 people, and 71 persons by the surname of Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all I have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It appears that the Prosecution is proceeding quickly through their rebuttal. So, Mr. Kay, if the Defence has any rejoinder we would like you to be prepared to begin perhaps on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the other matter relates to the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witness AA. Is there any significance to that? I do not want to discuss it in open session, but just find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand there is no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No opposition, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. That will be granted. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The Court adjourned until the following day).
